**How to make sure you’re not holding onto anything that belongs to someone else**

Below is a short, step‑by‑step process that pulls together the advice from the “borrowed‑item‑tracking” material in the knowledge base [[summaries/session-15_2025-02-15]] and the related concepts [[concepts/borrowed-item-tracking]], [[concepts/reminder-system]], [[concepts/visual-cue-logging]].

| Step | What to do | Why it helps |
|------|------------|--------------|
| **1. Gather everything in one place** | Designate a single, obvious spot (a shelf, basket, or drawer) for all items you suspect might be borrowed. | Having a “single‑view” location makes it easy to see what isn’t yours at a glance. |
| **2. Create a visual record** | For each item, take a quick photo with your phone and write a one‑sentence note (e.g., “Jane’s black scarf – borrowed 22 Feb”). Save the photo‑note pair in a simple folder or notes app. | The picture + note acts as a visual cue (concept [[concepts/visual-cue-logging]]) so the item stays on your radar even if you forget the name of the owner. |
| **3. Add a calendar reminder** | Create a calendar event or phone reminder for each item. If you know the return date, set that exact date; if not, set a recurring weekly “Check borrowed items” reminder. | The reminder (concept [[concepts/reminder-system]]) forces you to review the list regularly. |
| **4. Perform a weekly “check‑in”** | When the weekly reminder fires, open your photo‑note folder, scan the items, and ask yourself: “Do I have a meeting or conversation scheduled with the owner soon?” If not, it’s safe to reach out. | Periodic check‑ins prevent items from slipping into the background. |
| **5. Reach out with a casual, friendly message** | Use a short template like one of the examples from the source (e.g., “Hey [Name]! I still have your [item] – would it be easiest for me to drop it off at your place or should I bring it next time we meet?”). Adjust the tone to match your relationship. | A low‑pressure text (the “casual return communication” suggestion) lets the owner know you’re thinking of them without sounding demanding. |
| **6. Log the outcome** | Once the item is returned, delete its photo‑note and mark the reminder as completed. If you arrange a later drop‑off, update the note with the new date. | Keeping the log tidy ensures you don’t chase the same item twice. |

**What you have right now**

The knowledge base only contains the *methodology* for tracking borrowed items; it does **not** list any specific items you are currently holding. In other words, you have the following tools ready to use:

- A visual‑cue system (photos + notes) – [[concepts/visual-cue-logging]]  
- A reminder workflow (calendar or phone alerts) – [[concepts/reminder-system]]  
- Sample casual‑return text templates (see the “Casual return communication” bullet in the summary).  

If you want a concrete inventory of what you’re currently holding, you’ll need to start the process above: gather the items, take the photos, and record the notes. Once you’ve entered a few entries, the system itself will become the “what do I have now” list you can refer to and update.
